bibliography.checked_against: Crossref and the title page ('Journal of Fish Biology (2006) 69, 461–472')
bibliography.note: authors, year, title, volume and pages match; the issue (2) is from Crossref (the PDF does not print it)

claims.claim: among pike, cannibalism falls mainly on young-of-year (and yearlings) and can regulate density
claims.quote: recruitment of YOY pike to 1 year-old pike is controlled by cannibalism
claims.conditions: a theoretical expectation (Claessen et al. 2002; Persson et al. 2004) that the authors take the stable length structure of three Italian stream pike populations (1985–1993) to support; p. 470 adds that cannibalism 'has been suggested to be an important regulating mechanism' (citing Persson et al. 2000, Soupir et al. 2000, Skov & Koed 2004)
claims.note: This source names young-of-year as the victims ('eaten at a very early stage'); it does not mention yearlings, which must come from Craig 2008 if anywhere. The regulation is inferred from population patterns, not measured.

claims.claim: conspecifics are a minor part of the cannibal pike's diet
claims.location: p. 470 (PDF p. 10); Table II, p. 469 (PDF p. 9)
claims.quote: their prey only make up a minor fraction of the cannibal's diet
claims.conditions: a general statement for 'systems where cannibals impose a high mortality on their prey' (citing Claessen et al. 2000; Persson et al. 2003). In the paper's own stream data pike occurred in 0–14 % of stomachs by length class (stream 1: 0 % <15 cm, 10 % 15–30 cm, 13 % 30–45 cm, n = 43/40/8; stream 3: 14 % at 30–45 cm, n = 14; none in stream 2)

claims.claim: in Swedish lakes the fish prey of pike, conspecifics included, were 0.03–0.55 of the predator's length
claims.location: p. 465 (PDF p. 5), Results 'Piscivory windows of pike and perch'; methods p. 464 (PDF p. 4)
claims.quote: minimum size ratio was lower (0·03) for pike … upper size ratio was higher (0·55)
claims.conditions: Lakes Abborrtjärn 1 and 2, middle Sweden; ≥ 20 pike of 50–600 mm total length sampled weekly in each lake, end of May to end of August 2002; prey (perch and pike) lengths from measured prey and length–mass regressions; the 0.03 and 0.55 are the lower and upper boundaries of piscivory drawn on the diet data (Claessen et al. 2000), prey:predator total length; t-tests against perch's 0.05 and 0.45, n = 4, P = 0.01
claims.note: The boundaries are of the whole piscivory window (cannibalism plus predation on perch), drawn as limits rather than single observed extremes.

claims.claim: pike take conspecifics to 0.55 of their length
claims.source_value: 0.55 is the upper boundary of pike's piscivory window as a whole — perch prey and cannibalism together — in Lakes Abborrtjärn 1 and 2 (2002); no separate limit is given for conspecific prey
claims.quote: Piscivory in pike involved both cannibalism and predation on perch
claims.conditions: as above: two small Swedish lakes, summer 2002, pike 50–600 mm
claims.note: Reword the comment to 'pike take fish prey, conspecifics included, to 0.55 (Persson et al. 2006)'.

notes: The paper's main study is of three small spring-fed streams in the Venetian plain, north-east Italy (Vicenza; 0.48–0.53 m mean depth, 2.5–5.7 m wide, 9–14 °C year-round), sampled each spawning season 1985–1993: pike length structure and cohort growth varied little between years, unlike Abborrtjärn 3's perch. Only the piscivory-window comparison comes from Swedish lakes, so §3.7.7's 'In Swedish lakes' is right. Other values: von Bertalanffy L∞ 321–353 mm in the closed stream 1, 1,004 mm (males) and 1,603 mm (females) in stream 3 (Fig. 2, p. 467); in stream 1, 84 % of pike < 15 cm had eaten only invertebrates, falling to 50 % at 30–45 cm (p. 467, Table II). Perch's own cannibal window is 0.05–0.45 (p. 465), which matches Persson et al. 2004's δ and ε.
